questions.stem: Two days after starting induction chemotherapy for acute leukemia with a very high white cell count, a client has a potassium of 6.4 mEq/L, a phosphorus of 7.2 mg/dL, a calcium of 7.0 mg/dL, a high uric acid and falling urine output. Which condition does the nurse suspect?

options.text: Tumor lysis syndrome
Hypercalcemia of malignancy
Syndrome of inappropriate ADH
Dehydration from vomiting

rationale.correct: Tumor lysis syndrome: prevent it with aggressive hydration and allopurinol or rasburicase, and monitor electrolytes and kidney function.

perOption.a: Rapid cell breakdown releases potassium, phosphorus and uric acid, and phosphorus binds calcium.
perOption.b: The calcium is low, not high.
perOption.c: SIADH causes hyponatremia, not this pattern.
perOption.d: This does not explain the electrolyte pattern.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A 64-year-old client with small-cell lung cancer reports that the collar of the shirt feels tight. The nurse notes swelling of the face and both arms, distended neck veins and shortness of breath when lying flat. Which condition does the nurse suspect?

options.text: Superior vena cava syndrome
Right-sided heart failure
An allergic reaction to chemotherapy
Community-acquired pneumonia

rationale.correct: SVC syndrome: keep the client upright, give oxygen and prepare for radiation or stenting.

perOption.a: A tumor in the mediastinum blocks blood return from the upper body.
perOption.b: Heart failure causes swelling of the legs, not the face and arms.
perOption.c: This does not fit the slow onset and pattern.
perOption.d: Pneumonia does not cause facial and arm swelling.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old client with prostate cancer that has spread to the spine reports new, worsening back pain over 3 days and says the legs feel weak and heavy. This morning the client had trouble starting to urinate. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Report it at once as possible spinal cord compression
Apply a heating pad to the back and reassess the pain tomorrow
Encourage more walking to keep the legs strong
Document it as expected bone pain from the cancer

rationale.correct: Spinal cord compression: new back pain with neurological or bladder changes is an emergency.

perOption.a: Early treatment with steroids and radiation can prevent permanent paralysis.
perOption.b: Delay risks paralysis.
perOption.c: This is not appropriate and may cause a fall.
perOption.d: New weakness and urinary changes are red flags.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize spinal cord compression in cancer.

questions.stem: A client 9 days after chemotherapy for lymphoma has an ANC of 300/mm3 and a temperature of 38.4 °C (101.1 °F). The client feels well apart from tiredness, and the blood pressure is 118/72. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Notify the provider, draw cultures; antibiotics within 1 hour
Give acetaminophen and recheck the temperature again in 4 hours
Wait for the culture results before starting any antibiotic
Encourage fluids and rest, and recheck in the morning

rationale.correct: Neutropenic fever (38.3 °C once, or 38.0 °C sustained, with an ANC below 500): cultures and antibiotics within 1 hour.

perOption.a: Neutropenic fever is an emergency, and sepsis can develop quickly even when the client looks well.
perOption.b: Delaying antibiotics increases mortality.
perOption.c: Antibiotics are not delayed for results.
perOption.d: This is not enough.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client receiving 5-fluorouracil has painful mouth sores and is eating very little. Which instruction should the nurse give?

options.text: Rinse with saline or baking soda and use a soft toothbrush
Rinse with an alcohol-based mouthwash to kill the germs quickly
Eat spicy or acidic foods to help the appetite
Brush with a firm toothbrush to keep plaque away

rationale.correct: Mucositis: gentle oral care, bland soft foods, no alcohol or tobacco, and topical anesthetics as prescribed.

perOption.a: Gentle rinses clean the mouth and reduce irritation.
perOption.b: Alcohol dries and irritates the mucosa.
perOption.c: Spicy and acidic foods irritate sores.
perOption.d: This injures the mucosa.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client is about to receive cisplatin, a highly emetogenic chemotherapy drug, at 1000. Ondansetron, dexamethasone and aprepitant are prescribed. When should the nurse give the antiemetics?

options.text: Before the chemotherapy infusion starts
Only if the client vomits during the infusion
On the day after the chemotherapy is given
At bedtime, after the infusion has finished

rationale.correct: Give antiemetics before chemotherapy and continue them as scheduled for delayed nausea.

perOption.a: Preventing nausea works far better than treating it.
perOption.b: Prevention is more effective.
perOption.c: Some doses continue for days, but the first doses come before.
perOption.d: This does not cover the infusion.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information

questions.stem: A 58-year-old client with breast cancer is receiving doxorubicin. Before the fourth cycle, the client reports new shortness of breath when climbing stairs, needing two pillows at night and ankle swelling. The total dose received so far is near the lifetime limit, and the client has a history of hypertension. Which adverse effect does the nurse suspect?

options.text: Cardiotoxicity
Hypoglycemia
Ototoxicity
Nephrotoxicity

rationale.correct: Doxorubicin: cardiotoxicity, myelosuppression, harmless red urine, and it is a vesicant.

perOption.a: Doxorubicin can cause dose-related heart failure; heart function is checked before and during treatment.
perOption.b: This is not a key effect of doxorubicin.
perOption.c: Hearing loss is more typical of cisplatin.
perOption.d: This does not explain dyspnea and ankle swelling.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client with testicular cancer is scheduled to receive cisplatin. The creatinine is normal. Which intervention helps prevent kidney injury from the drug?

options.text: Generous IV hydration before and after the infusion
Restricting fluids to 1 L on the day of the infusion
Giving ibuprofen for any discomfort during treatment
Holding the antiemetics to reduce the drug load

rationale.correct: Cisplatin: nephrotoxicity, ototoxicity, nausea and electrolyte loss, especially magnesium.

perOption.a: Hydration dilutes cisplatin and protects the kidneys.
perOption.b: This increases the risk of kidney injury.
perOption.c: NSAIDs increase kidney risk.
perOption.d: This is not related to kidney protection.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A child receiving vincristine for acute lymphoblastic leukemia has numbness and tingling in the fingers, trouble buttoning a shirt and no bowel movement for 4 days. What do these findings suggest?

options.text: Neurotoxicity from the vincristine
Hypercalcemia from the leukemia
An allergic reaction to the drug
Expected signs of improvement

rationale.correct: Vincristine: peripheral neuropathy and constipation; report worsening symptoms and use a bowel regimen.

perOption.a: Vincristine causes peripheral neuropathy and autonomic effects such as constipation.
perOption.b: This does not explain the numbness.
perOption.c: This does not fit.
perOption.d: These are adverse effects.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client is in the second week of external beam radiation to the chest and asks about skin care. Which statement by the client shows a need for more teaching?

options.text: "I'll wash the area gently with lukewarm water and a mild soap."
"I'll scrub off the ink markings when I take a shower."
"I'll keep the area covered and out of the sun."
"I'll wear loose cotton shirts over the treated area."

rationale.correct: Radiation skin care: gentle washing, keep the markings, avoid lotions unless prescribed, and avoid sun, heat and cold.

perOption.a: This is appropriate.
perOption.b: The markings guide treatment and must not be removed.
perOption.c: Irradiated skin burns easily.
perOption.d: This reduces irritation.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Teach skin care during radiation therapy.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old client starting a chemotherapy regimen that usually causes hair loss says, "I don't want my kids to see me bald." What is the nurse's best response?

options.text: "Hair loss is usually temporary; let's talk about wigs and scarves."
"Don't worry, many people on this treatment keep most of their hair."
"Hair loss from this treatment is usually permanent."
"Your hair isn't important compared with beating the cancer."

rationale.correct: Alopecia affects body image; give accurate information and practical options, and include the family as the client wishes.

perOption.a: This gives accurate information and supports coping.
perOption.b: This may be false reassurance for this regimen.
perOption.c: It is usually temporary.
perOption.d: This dismisses the client's feelings.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Support a client facing chemotherapy-related hair loss.

questions.stem: A client is going home after a left mastectomy with axillary lymph node removal. Which instruction should the nurse give?

options.text: "Don't allow blood pressures or blood draws on your left arm."
"Keep your left arm still and in a sling for the next 6 months."
"Carry your grocery bags on the left side to build strength."
"Expect the left arm to stay swollen for the rest of your life."

rationale.correct: After lymph node removal: protect the arm, do the prescribed exercises and report swelling.

perOption.a: This reduces the risk of lymphedema and infection.
perOption.b: Gradual exercise is encouraged.
perOption.c: Heavy loads increase lymphedema risk.
perOption.d: Lymphedema can often be prevented or managed.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A 42-year-old woman with no family history of breast cancer asks when she should have screening mammograms. What is the nurse's best response, based on current USPSTF guidance?

options.text: "Every 2 years, starting at age 40."
"Once a year, starting after age 60."
"If you or your doctor feel a lump, not before."
"Every 5 years, starting at age 50."

rationale.correct: Mammography every 2 years from 40 to 74 (USPSTF 2024); other organizations may advise yearly screening.

perOption.a: USPSTF recommends mammography every 2 years from 40 to 74 for average-risk women.
perOption.b: This starts too late.
perOption.c: Screening is for women without symptoms.
perOption.d: This is not the recommendation.

references: U.S. Preventive Services Task Force recommendations
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A 19-year-old man asks the nurse how to check his testicles for cancer. When should he do the self-exam?

options.text: Monthly, after a warm shower
Yearly, in a cool room
After he turns 50
When there is pain

rationale.correct: Testicular self-exam: monthly after a warm shower; report painless lumps or heaviness.

perOption.a: Warmth relaxes the scrotum, making lumps easier to feel.
perOption.b: Cold tightens the scrotum.
perOption.c: Testicular cancer is most common between 15 and 35.
perOption.d: Testicular cancer is often painless.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old client with a cervix who had a normal Pap test 3 years ago asks how often to have cervical cancer screening. What is the nurse's best response?

options.text: "A Pap test every 3 years."
"A Pap test every year."
"Not until you turn 30."
"If you have symptoms."

rationale.correct: Cervical screening: 21 to 29, Pap every 3 years; 30 to 65, HPV testing every 5 years or other approved options.

perOption.a: Ages 21 to 29: cytology every 3 years.
perOption.b: Annual screening is not recommended for average risk.
perOption.c: Screening starts at 21.
perOption.d: Screening is for people without symptoms.

references: U.S. Preventive Services Task Force recommendations
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old client with newly diagnosed acute myeloid leukemia has a WBC of 48,000/mm3 with many blasts, a hemoglobin of 8.1 g/dL and platelets of 22,000/mm3. Which nursing problem is the priority?

options.text: Risk for infection
Disturbed body image
Lack of knowledge
Risk for constipation

rationale.correct: Acute leukemia: infection and bleeding risks are the priorities, despite a high white cell count.

perOption.a: Immature white cells do not fight infection, and infection is a leading cause of death.
perOption.b: This is a lower priority.
perOption.c: This is a lower priority.
perOption.d: This is a lower priority.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old client has had night sweats, a weight loss of 5 kg and fevers for 2 months. Which finding on examination is typical of Hodgkin lymphoma?

options.text: A painless, rubbery lymph node above the collarbone
A tender, red neck lymph node with a sore throat
Bone pain with a rising creatinine and anemia
Easy bruising and bleeding of the gums

rationale.correct: Hodgkin lymphoma: painless lymph node swelling, sometimes with fever, night sweats and weight loss (B symptoms).

perOption.a: Painless lymphadenopathy, often in the neck, is the classic presentation.
perOption.b: This suggests infection.
perOption.c: This suggests multiple myeloma.
perOption.d: This suggests leukemia or low platelets.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old client with multiple myeloma has back and rib pain, a calcium of 12.4 mg/dL and a creatinine that has risen from 1.1 to 1.8 mg/dL. The client has no fluid restriction. Which intervention is most important?

options.text: Encourage 2 to 3 L of fluid a day
Keep the client on strict bed rest
Limit fluids to protect the kidneys
Offer a high-calcium diet to help strengthen the weak bones

rationale.correct: Multiple myeloma: bone pain, fractures, hypercalcemia and kidney failure; hydration and fall safety are key.

perOption.a: Fluids help clear calcium and protect the kidneys from protein damage.
perOption.b: Immobility increases calcium loss from bone.
perOption.c: This worsens kidney damage.
perOption.d: This worsens hypercalcemia.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client with metastatic pancreatic cancer has constant abdominal pain rated 6 to 7 out of 10 that wakes the client at night. The client takes oxycodone 5 mg only when the pain becomes severe. Which change would the nurse expect?

options.text: Scheduled long-acting opioid plus a breakthrough dose
Keep giving the oxycodone when the pain is severe
Switch to ibuprofen to avoid opioid addiction
Give saline injections to see if the pain is real

rationale.correct: Cancer pain: around-the-clock dosing, breakthrough doses and preventing side effects such as constipation.

perOption.a: Steady levels stop the pain returning, and breakthrough doses treat flares.
perOption.b: This leads to poor control.
perOption.c: Opioids are appropriate for cancer pain.
perOption.d: Placebo injections are unethical.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client in the last hours of life has noisy, gurgling breathing. The client is unresponsive and appears comfortable, but the family is upset by the sound. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Turn the client to the side; give the prescribed glycopyrrolate
Suction deep into the airway every hour to clear the secretions
Increase the IV fluid rate to thin out the secretions in the throat
Ask the family to wait outside until the noisy breathing stops

rationale.correct: Terminal secretions ('death rattle') are managed with positioning and anticholinergics such as glycopyrrolate, along with family support.

perOption.a: Positioning and drying secretions reduce the noise; the nurse explains that it is common near death.
perOption.b: Deep suctioning is distressing and usually not effective.
perOption.c: More fluid increases secretions.
perOption.d: Family presence is supportive.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client with end-stage heart failure is actively dying in a hospice unit, and the family is at the bedside. Which comfort measures should the nurse provide? Select all that apply.

options.text: Frequent mouth care
Repositioning for comfort
Medication for pain and breathlessness
Encouraging family to stay and touch
Insisting the client eat full meals
Limiting visits to 10 minutes

rationale.correct: End-of-life care focuses on comfort, dignity and family support.

perOption.a: Mouth breathing dries the mucosa.
perOption.b: This prevents discomfort and skin breakdown.
perOption.c: Comfort is the goal.
perOption.d: This supports the client and family.
perOption.e: Appetite naturally falls; forcing food causes discomfort.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Provide comfort care at the end of life.

questions.stem: The case manager is reviewing four clients for hospice referral. Which client meets the usual criteria for hospice care?

options.text: A client whose provider certifies a life expectancy of 6 months or less
A client with newly diagnosed cancer that is likely to be cured
A client with heart failure who wants a heart transplant sometime next year
A client expected to live a few more days, and no longer

rationale.correct: Hospice: a prognosis of 6 months or less if the disease follows its usual course, with care focused on comfort.

perOption.a: This is the standard eligibility rule.
perOption.b: Eligibility depends on prognosis, not on the diagnosis.
perOption.c: Hospice focuses on comfort rather than cure.
perOption.d: Hospice is not limited to the last days; earlier referral is better.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client with expected death from lung cancer has just died in the hospital. No autopsy is planned, and it is not a coroner's case. The family is in the waiting room. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Remove lines per policy, clean the body and invite the family in
Send the body to the morgue right away to free up the room
Leave the tubes and lines in place for the funeral home
Ask the family to go home and come back once the nurse has finished the care

rationale.correct: Postmortem care: follow policy, maintain dignity and support the family.

perOption.a: Postmortem care preserves dignity and supports grieving.
perOption.b: The family should have time with the client.
perOption.c: Tubes are left in only for an autopsy or coroner's case.
perOption.d: The family may wish to stay or help.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client will take oral capecitabine at home. The client's spouse will help, and their adult daughter, who is pregnant, visits often. Select the 3 safety instructions the nurse should give.

options.text: Wear gloves to handle the tablets or body fluids
Flush the toilet twice after the client uses it
Wash soiled linens separately from other laundry
Crush the tablets if they are hard to swallow
Ask the daughter to help set out the doses
Keep the tablets with the family's other pills

rationale.correct: Oral chemotherapy is hazardous; protect caregivers from exposure, especially for about 48 hours after doses.

perOption.a: Chemotherapy is excreted in body fluids.
perOption.b: This reduces exposure for others.
perOption.c: This prevents contamination.
perOption.d: Crushing releases hazardous particles.
perOption.f: They are stored separately and safely.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Teach home safety for oral chemotherapy.
